GILD Miami this past Monday was a good reminder that the quality of a room has less to do with how many people are in it and more to do with how willing they are to engage with each other.

The conversation started with Alexandria de Aranzeta, JD (Data & AI Governance Policy, Boeing), who challenged the room to think about AI progress beyond sheer activity. More code, more experiments, and faster development do not necessarily translate into more value. The real question is where an organization sits on the path from experimentation to repeatable, scaled execution, and whether teams are measuring the things that actually matter.

That framing opened up a much broader conversation across the room, but what stood out most was how people participated. There was very little posturing and a lot of specificity. Leaders shared what they are trying, where things are getting stuck, and what they are still figuring out. Conversations kept carrying over between groups, introductions happened naturally, and people stayed engaged well beyond the initial discussion.

Miami is becoming a particularly interesting GILD community for us because of that mix. Different industries, company stages, and perspectives, but a shared willingness to compare notes openly and get into the substance of the work.

GILD Austin Event: a room of engineering leaders working through something most teams feel but haven't named the comprehension gap.

AI has decoupled how fast we ship from how well we understand what we shipped. Pre-AI, understanding was baked into the build process slow, but built in. Now delivery has outpaced comprehension, and the cost that used to hide inside the build cycle is sitting out in the open.

Our conversation starter, Ivan Pointer (Senior Director of Engineering, NetRise), walked the room through a live case study a two-phase RBAC rewrite where phase one shipped clean, and phase two stalled entirely: thousands of lines of spec churn, dozens of commits, most of them reverts. Not because the team got worse. Because the agents and the humans were now contending with a system too large to hold in their heads.

The best ideas in the room were ownership structures: engineers accountable for what they ship, constraint limits on how much a single PR can touch, weekly sessions where the team has to explain their own code out loud.

The room brought together leaders from companies including Oracle, Dell Technologies, Global Payments, Sonar, SmartAsset, Atlassian, and others across AI, software, cybersecurity, and enterprise technology.

The open question on the table: how do you keep development deterministic when "done" becomes a vibe instead of a test case.

AI monitoring tells you a system is running. It doesn't tell you whether to trust what it's doing.

That's the distinction engineering leaders keep running into as AI moves from pilot to production. Monitoring answers "did the call succeed." Observability answers "was the output good enough to trust."

Token cost. Output quality. Prompt and context traces. Drift. Human feedback loops. That's the operating view technical leaders now need in one place, not scattered across five dashboards.
